questions.question: Why can't embeddings produced by two different embedding models be directly compared for similarity search?
options: All embedding models produce identical, interchangeable vectors
Different models are trained differently and optimize for different notions of similarity, so their vectors aren't comparable to each other
Embeddings can only be compared if they are exactly one dimension
This is never actually a real constraint in practice
questions.explanation: Each embedding model learns its own representation of meaning, so vectors from different models exist in different, incompatible spaces and cannot be meaningfully compared for similarity.

questions.question: What does 're-indexing' mean when an embedding model is changed?
options: Renaming files in the vector database
Re-embedding every existing chunk in the corpus with the new model, since old embeddings aren't compatible with it
Deleting the vector database entirely with no replacement
Changing only the database's search algorithm, not the data
questions.explanation: Because embeddings from different models aren't comparable, switching embedding models requires re-embedding (re-indexing) the entire existing document corpus — a real, sometimes significant compute and time cost.

questions.question: A RAG system performs poorly on internal engineering documentation full of specific jargon. Which question best identifies a likely, targeted fix?
options: Should we conclude that RAG as an approach is fundamentally broken?
Have we benchmarked our current embedding model against domain-specific alternatives, since a general-purpose model may not capture our jargon well?
Should we abandon retrieval entirely and rely only on the LLM's built-in knowledge?
Is this definitely a chunking problem and nothing else?
questions.explanation: Poor performance on specialized/jargon-heavy content is a classic symptom of an embedding model mismatch, which is a specific, benchmarkable, and fixable issue rather than evidence that RAG itself doesn't work.
